book.title: Her Şey Yolunda (Everything Is F*cked: A Book About Hope)
book.author: Mark Manson

confidence_note: Manson argues across his books that more options do not bring more happiness and that freedom comes through commitment or self-limitation; the fullest treatment with Barry Schwartz's 'paradox of choice' and his own years of travel and short-term dating is in The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck, so those details are not used as facts for this book. In Everything Is F*cked he criticizes a shallow 'fake freedom' of endless choice and argues true freedom involves self-limitation, which is kept at a general level. The TR quote and the claim that 'research consistently shows' more choice means less happiness are not verified for this book and are excluded. Not checked against the text.
facts: Manson contrasts a shallow freedom of endless options with a deeper freedom that comes from choosing what to give up.
He argues that keeping every option open prevents depth in any one relationship, career or pursuit.
In his view, commitment necessarily involves loss, closing off alternatives, and that loss is the price of depth and meaning.
No specific case from this book is used; the facts describe the argument only.
tension: Closing doors feels like losing freedom, yet Manson argues that refusing to close any is what keeps life shallow.
opening_idea: Start with a person keeping every door open, several half-started paths at once, and ask what they're actually free to do in any of them.

lessons.idea: More options can feel like freedom while preventing depth.
lessons.anchor: Manson's contrast between fake freedom and self-limitation

lessons.idea: Commitment means accepting a loss, and that loss is what buys depth.
lessons.anchor: the argument that commitment closes alternatives

reflect: Where are you keeping options open mainly to avoid choosing?
What have you gained from something you committed to despite giving up alternatives?
reflect_final: Choose one open option you've been keeping 'just in case' and deliberately close it this week; afterward, notice what attention it frees up.

use_cases.situation: A roadmap has ten 'priority' items and nothing ships.
use_cases.move: Propose cutting to two commitments for the quarter and writing down which options you're explicitly giving up.

use_cases.situation: A friend keeps swiping on dating apps while seeing someone they like.
use_cases.move: Ask what they'd gain by closing the other options for a while, following Manson's point that depth needs self-limitation.

use_cases.situation: You're spreading free time across several side projects.
use_cases.move: Pick one, archive the others' notes in a folder, and give the chosen one your next free block.

pocket_idea: An open door you never walk through still costs you a glance every day; closing some is how you finally go through one.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Manson argues the freest thing you can do is choose what to give up.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Manson contrasts the shallow freedom of endless options with the deeper freedom of self-limitation: commitment closes doors and feels like loss, but that loss is what makes depth possible.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What's something you committed to that only became meaningful after you stopped looking at alternatives?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: Keeping every option open versus choosing one and letting the rest go.
